To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
methane emissions from sheep are approximately 10 g head(-1) day(-1), and that the emission is approximately proportional to the amount of feed eaten.
the methane emission from sheep grazing is approximately 5.1 +/- 1.1 kg per animal per year, and that the measurement of methane losses by sheep is feasible under grazing conditions.
the average emission rate of methane by grazing animals was estimated to be 5.1 ± 0.4 kg year(-1), with a range from 4.0 to 6.0 kg year(-1).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the measurement and control of emissions of greenhouse gases from agricultural sources.
the development and application of techniques which allow the measurement of the emission of greenhouse gases from agricultural livestock.
the development of a technique for estimating the emission of methane from sheep grazing in field conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
methane emission from the sheep grazing in this study is 14 g day-1 animal-1.
sheep grazing in the UK emit 1.5% of the total UK methane emissions, which is equivalent to 1% of total greenhouse gas emissions.
the methane emissions from sheep, although lower than many estimates, are still significant and should be included in the total methane budget for UK agriculture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
methane emission rates from sheep are approximately 10 times higher than the rates from cows.
the methane emission from sheep grazing in this country is about 1.2 x 10(6) tonnes year(-1) and that the total methane emission from UK agriculture is about 2.4 x 10(7) tonnes year(-l).
the emission of methane by sheep is of similar order of magnitude to that of ruminant cattle and is of the same magnitude as emissions by sheep from enteric fermentation.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the measurement of methane emissions from grazing sheep is possible and should be undertaken in order to provide more accurate estimates of methane emissions from sheep and to assess the effectiveness of mitigation strategies.

the use of a portable, lightweight system to measure the methane emissions of grazing sheep is a practical, reliable and cost-effective method for obtaining methane emission rates for use in national inventories.
it is possible to measure methane emissions directly from grazing animals in the field and the system described is sufficiently robust to allow such measurements to be made routinely.
